Summary

NGS-DOSE measures the copy number of the 45S and 5S ribosomal DNA arrays, and of other sequence that reference genomes collapse, from aligned short-read genomes, which exist for hundreds of thousands of people. Standard analysis of those files does not report it, long-read assemblies leave the arrays in pieces, and read-depth ratios measure the library along with the person (section 1). Reads are assigned to a sequence class by class-specific 31-mers and counted as fragment ends; a per-library model of fragment-GC bias, fitted on 800 single-copy control regions, gives the expected count of any sequence, and the windows of the rDNA unit are calibrated across the cohort. An assay of rDNA copy number (ddPCR) exists for only a dozen of these lines, so the measurement is validated against sequence of known copy number in every genome, inheritance in trios, the same individuals sequenced on two technologies, independent measurements of the same files, and the assay where it exists.

In 1,259 genomes, held-out autosomal sequence reads 1.998 ± 0.008 copies (expected 2); chrX reads 0.991 ± 0.007 in men with one X and 1.937 ± 0.027 in women with an intact culture (expected 1 and 2); chrY reads 0.978 ± 0.028 in men and at most 0.010 in women (expected 1 and 0). Sex inferred from the reads agrees with the pedigree in 1,258 of 1,259. The distal junction, present once on each acrocentric short arm, reads 9.674 ± 0.341 (expected 10); departures from the cohort's level are whole copies (74 carriers), transmitted in 14 of 37 carrier-parent–child pairs and de novo in 1. The targeted fetch returns 0.9997 of the whole-file scan's 45S estimate (1,259 genomes; range 0.9988–0.9999). Run on the fetch counts alone, the cohort layer and the trio test give the same answer: 45S reliability 1.00 (0.93–1.21) against 1.00 from the scans.

In 252 trios the calibrated 45S estimate has a transmission reliability of 1.00 (0.93–1.21); traits that are not transmitted read near zero (held-out autosomal sequence -0.06, mitochondrial content 0.11). In 12 individuals sequenced on two technologies, the test–retest intraclass correlation is 0.98 for NGS-DOSE's calibrated estimate and 0.19 for the 18S depth ratio of published studies, computed from the same reads for comparison (0.87 after removing its offset between technologies). Within one chemistry the published depth ratio follows each library's GC bias (r = 0.85); under NGS-DOSE's fragment-GC model it does not (r = 0.07). Against ddPCR (Potapova et al. 2025) on 12 lymphoblastoid lines, NGS-DOSE reads 0.96× the assay (r = 0.95); CONKORD, the authors' k-mer estimate from their own reads, 0.99× (r = 0.87); the 18S depth ratio 1.09× (r = 0.93). Against the published estimates of Hall et al. (2021) for the same files, r = 0.985 on 954 shared samples; their exclusion of duplicate-flagged reads accounts for the offset. NGS-PCA's coverage-based mitochondrial copy number for the same files agrees with ours at r = 0.996 (theirs 0.92× ours, the duplicate flag again), its chrX ratio at r = 0.9997. 1 of 10 satellite families track HPRC assemblies of 96 of these individuals with r ≥ 0.95.

What is not shown: the absolute scale of the rDNA rests on unit windows on which three Illumina chemistries agree, not on an assay; every sample is a lymphoblastoid cell line sequenced with one chemistry and one pipeline.

1. Rationale

Each human genome carries several hundred copies of the 45S ribosomal DNA unit, about 45 kb long, in tandem arrays on the short arms of the five acrocentric chromosomes, and a tandem array of the 5S unit on chromosome 1. A single array spans from 50 kb to more than 6 Mb, the two homologues of a chromosome almost never carry arrays of one size, and an array is rearranged in more than one meiosis in ten (Stults et al., Genome Res 2008). Total copy number varies severalfold between individuals and is heritable.

Why a method is needed

Short-read genomes are the only genomes that exist at population scale: 490,640 in UK Biobank alone (UK Biobank Whole-Genome Sequencing Consortium, Nature 2025), where rDNA copy number estimated from them has been associated with blood-cell counts and kidney function (Rodriguez-Algarra, Evans & Rakyan, Cell Genomics 2024) and with metabolic disease (Raj et al., medRxiv 2026, a preprint). At that size a correlation of 0.01 between an estimate and a trait has p ≈ 2 × 10−12, so whatever an estimate carries of the library, rather than the person, becomes a finding wherever the library also tracks the trait. Standard analysis does not give the number, and read-depth ratios, long reads and laboratory assays each fall short on scale or on the library (below). What is needed is a measurement that finds every rDNA read wherever the aligner put it (3.3), predicts each library's count of GC-rich sequence from single-copy sequence in the same genome (3.5), holds its scale across chemistries (3.4), does not depend on the duplicate flag (3.7), reads a small part of each file (3.3), and shows in every genome that it reads known copy numbers correctly (3.1, 3.2). NGS-DOSE is one way to meet these, and the tests on this page apply to any other. The 18S depth ratio of published studies is not NGS-DOSE's estimate: it is computed from the same reads and carried beside it throughout as the comparator, and wherever the two can be told apart, across technologies (3.4) and across libraries' GC bias (3.5), NGS-DOSE does better.

Standard analysis
Reports no copy number. GRCh38 carries fewer than ten copies of the 45S transcribed region, on chr21 and two small contigs, where a genome has hundreds; the reads of every unit fall on those copies with no unique alignment, and variant and copy-number callers mask the loci.
Read-depth ratio
Depth on the reference's rDNA relative to depth elsewhere in the genome, as in published studies (Gibbons et al., Nat Commun 2014; Hall et al., Sci Rep 2021; Rodriguez-Algarra et al. 2024), runs on existing files. Without a model of the library it measures the library along with the person: the rDNA is GC-rich, parts of the unit drop out by amounts that depend on the chemistry, and the duplicate flag marks 5.3% of 45S reads against 9.5% of single-copy reads, so dropping flagged reads moves the ratio by a different amount in every genome (the two rates' ratio runs from 0.43 to 0.85). In UK Biobank its mean differs between the two sequencing centres (Rodriguez-Algarra et al. 2024). Here, within one chemistry the 18S ratio's departure from the calibrated estimate follows each library's GC bias (r = 0.85; 3.5); the same people read 27% lower by it on the older of two technologies (intraclass correlation 0.19, against 0.98 for the calibrated estimate; 3.4).
Long reads
The units are near-identical, which defeats assembly. Even in T2T-CHM13, three of the five arrays are model sequences, because ultra-long nanopore reads were not long enough to order their units (Nurk et al., Science 2022); in 156 acrocentric short arms assembled from HiFi, ultra-long nanopore and Hi-C data, the rDNA array collapsed in every one (Lin et al., Cell 2026). Long reads, imaging and methylation have given the size and activity of each array in fifteen genomes (Potapova et al., Cell Genomics 2025). Of the genomes counted here, 96 have an HPRC release-2 assembly; these hold 36% (22–71%) of the rDNA the measured copy number implies, in stretches no longer than 1.70 Mb, where the average array would be 2.2 Mb (data/rdna_hprc.tsv).
Molecular assays
Droplet digital PCR is precise (CHM13: 409 ± 9 copies; Nurk et al. 2022) and pulsed-field gels size single arrays (Stults et al. 2008), but each needs the DNA and a laboratory assay per person: in a biobank, every participant's stored DNA.

The case is strongest for the rDNA. Long-read assemblies close most satellite arrays and are their truth here (3.8), so for the satellites it is one of scale alone; telomeric content already has short-read estimators (Ding et al., Nucleic Acids Res 2014), and the class measured here is a relative one.

How the measurement is judged

Whether the measurement is correct cannot be settled by comparison with an assay, because none exists for these samples. It can be settled by comparison with what is known: (i) sequence of known copy number in every sample, measured by the same code; (ii) Mendelian transmission in the cohort's 602 trios; (iii) the same individuals sequenced on different technologies; (iv) an independent estimate from the same files; (v) long-read assemblies, for the satellite arrays measured by the same k-mer method. Each comparison excludes a different failure. The results are presented in that order.

2. Methods

Samples
The expanded 1000 Genomes cohort: 3,202 individuals in 26 populations, including 602 trios, sequenced by the New York Genome Center to about 30× (Illumina NovaSeq, 2×150 bp, PCR-free) and aligned to GRCh38 with decoy and HLA contigs (Byrska-Bishop et al., Cell 2022). All DNA is from lymphoblastoid cell lines. Counting runs on the public CRAMs; 1,259 genomes have been counted so far, 1,259 in both modes, with 252 of 602 trios complete.
Class assignment
Every 31-mer of every read is tested against a panel of class-diagnostic k-mers: k-mers of the class's unit sequence (45S, KY962518.1; 5S, X12811.1; distal junction, 400 kb of CHM13 chr21) that occur nowhere in GRCh38 or T2T-CHM13 outside the class's own loci. A read with at least four panel k-mers is assigned to the class and placed on the unit by its hits; its alignment position is not used. Experimental panels built from the CHM13 CenSat annotation add ten satellite families and the telomeric repeat.
Counting
Fragment 5′ ends are counted: per 50-bp bin and strand of the unit for class reads, and per position in 800 single-copy control regions (10.1 Mb) for the library model. Scan mode reads the whole CRAM; fetch mode retrieves only the control regions and 80 sink intervals (3.3 Mb) where the NYGC pipeline places class reads, learned from whole-file scans of two genomes.
Library model
A Poisson spline of fragment-end density on fragment GC content is fitted per sample on the control regions. The expected count of any sequence follows from its fragment-GC composition; the copy number of each 250-bp window of a unit is 2 × observed / expected (figure).
Calibration
Windows of the 45S unit drop out beyond what the GC curve predicts, by amounts that depend on the sequencing chemistry. Per-window efficiencies are learned across the cohort by median polish; the absolute scale is set by anchor windows on which three Illumina chemistries agreed in the pilot. Beside it the page carries NGS-DOSE's single-sample variant, from the anchor windows alone, and, as the comparator, the 18S read-depth ratio of published studies, with no GC model and no calibration: not NGS-DOSE's estimate (figure).
Estimators
Three 45S estimates travel through every table, two of them NGS-DOSE's. 45S, NGS-DOSE calibrated (rDNA45S.cn): the cohort model log Ciw = ci + aw + eiw over every retained 250-bp window w of the unit, fitted by median polish across samples i, with the window efficiencies aw pinned to a median of zero over the anchor windows; the estimate is exp(ci), so every window contributes precision and the anchors set the level. 45S, NGS-DOSE single-sample (rDNA45S.cn_single): 2 × observed / expected fragment ends summed over the anchor windows alone, under the sample's own fragment-GC model, with no information from any other sample. 45S, 18S depth ratio (published) (rDNA45S.18S.flat): 2 × fragment ends in the 18S gene / (positions × the control regions' mean rate), with no GC model and no calibration: the read-depth ratio of published studies, computed from the same reads as the comparator (figure). The 5S and distal-junction estimates are calibrated the same way as the 45S; the satellite masses are diploid megabases from the class's read count under the GC model.
Known-truth controls
80 held-out autosomal regions (two copies), 60 chrX regions (one in men, two in women) and 40 X-degenerate chrY regions (one, none), measured by the alignment-position path; and the distal junction, present once on each of the ten acrocentric short arms, measured by the k-mer path with its class restricted to k-mers that occur exactly once in each of the five CHM13 junctions. Mitochondrial genomes and EBV episomes per cell are measured as covariates of the culture.
Transmission
For each metric, values on the natural scale with the population mean subtracted; then, over the complete trios, the Pearson correlations of child with father, mother and midparent, the spousal (father–mother) correlation ρ, and the least-squares slope b of child on midparent. Reliability R = b − ρ(1 − b) estimates the share of the metric's variance that is transmitted (σ²T / (σ²T + σ²e)): 1 for a perfectly measured heritable trait, 0 for pure error. 95% intervals by family bootstrap at 20 trios or more; a one-sided p-value for the slope from 1,000 permutations of children among families; paired bootstrap for differences between estimators. Held-out autosomal sequence (no true variance) and mitochondrial and EBV content (not in the nuclear genome) are the negative controls.
Technical structure
Principal components of the control regions' residual depth after the GC model. The number retained is chosen at the Marchenko–Pastur edge of the noise bulk and checked by a cross-validated sweep against the known truths and the trios. NGS-PCA's genome-wide coverage PCs are applied where available.
External comparisons
The pilot's twelve genomes have an independent older library of the same cell line (HGSVC, HiSeq 2500 2×126, 2015; Illumina Platinum, HiSeq 2000 2×100, 2012–13), compared with anchor windows chosen with the family held out. Hall, Turner & Queitsch (Sci Rep 2021) published 18S copy number for 2,419 of these CRAMs as read depth relative to chromosome 1 with duplicate-flagged reads excluded. HPRC release-2 assemblies of cohort samples give the size of every satellite array (CenSat annotation, both haplotypes); a class is compared only where arrays containing gaps are immaterial. NGS-PCA's per-sample QC for the same cohort (mosdepth, 1-kb bins, duplicate-flagged reads excluded) gives mitochondrial copies per cell, the X and Y coverage ratios and the autosomal depth by a coverage route.
Provenance
Engine builds: 0.1.0+fae1124 (1,259). Resource bundle GRCh38-v1; panel 9ab0a0e8,a23ef9ed,7f3b4c3c, controls 184ab16e, sinks 9dd52ba1 (SHA-256 prefixes; one of each means one cohort). Read length 150; placement grid 1000 bp. Every input carried its end-of-file marker.

121 sample(s) carry a flag (aneuploid chromosome, sex mismatch, mosaic loss of an X or Y, a distal-junction step, low depth, another engine build); they are marked in the sample table and listed in data/flags.tsv. A flag marks something to examine, not a verdict.

3.1 Sequence of known copy number, in every genome

If the model is right, held-out autosomal sequence reads 2, chrX reads 1 in men and 2 in women, chrY reads 1 and 0, and the distal junction reads 10, in every genome. Held-out autosomal sequence reads 1.998 ± 0.008 copies (n = 1,259). chrX reads 0.991 ± 0.007 in 609 men with one X and 1.937 ± 0.027 in the 630 women whose culture has kept both X chromosomes (at least 1.85 copies); 19 women read below that. chrY reads 0.978 ± 0.028 in men with an intact Y and 0.0026 in women (maximum 0.0101); 9 men read below 0.85. One man reads two X chromosomes and a Y (HG01683: X 1.97, Y 0.97, X 1.97 by NGS-PCA's coverage ratio), as a 47,XXY karyotype would; he is left out of the men's mean and SD. The distal junction reads 9.674 ± 0.341 (cohort-calibrated). Women read the X and every genome reads the distal junction a few percent below expectation; both are late-replicating sequence, which DNA from a growing culture under-represents (section 4).

Sex inferred from the reads (a Y above 0.1 copies) agrees with the pedigree in 1,258 of 1,259 samples; it does not in HG02300 (a swapped sample, or a line that has lost its Y); NGS-PCA's coverage ratios read it the same way, so the discrepancy is in the sample or its record, not in this measurement.

3.2 The distal junction changes in whole copies, and the changes are inherited

Ten distal junctions is the norm; a rearranged acrocentric short arm leaves nine, and a Robertsonian translocation, which fuses two acrocentrics and loses both short arms, leaves eight. Copy number relative to the cohort's level (9.66) should therefore sit near a whole number, and a step, being a structural variant, should be transmitted to half of a carrier's children and arise de novo in almost none. Within ±0.3 of a step: 4 genomes at −2, 32 at −1, 1,030 at 0, 36 at +1; the main mode has a robust SD of 0.15 copies and 89 genomes sit between steps.

Where a carrier parent and a child were both counted, the step was transmitted in 14 of 37 (the expectation for a heterozygous variant is one half); HG01517 (+0.76 copies) carries a step that neither counted parent has: a new structural variant, or a change in part of the cell line. The distal junction is measured by the same k-mer path as the rDNA. A change of one copy in ten, seen in a parent and again in the child, shows that the path resolves multi-copy acrocentric sequence to a single copy.

Does the fetch carry the same information?

The cohort layer (window calibration, control-region PCs) and the trio test were run a second time on the fetch counts of the 1,259 genomes alone, without reference to the scans. 3.4 The same individuals on two sequencing technologies

The pilot's 12 genomes were also sequenced years earlier on a different instrument, with different read length, insert size, depth, alignment pipeline and a GC response the reverse of NovaSeq's. Agreement between the two libraries of a person, per estimator: NGS-DOSE's (the calibrated estimate with anchor windows chosen with the person's family held out, so the cross-technology level is out of sample) and, for comparison, the 18S depth ratio of published studies computed from the same reads:

The 5S unit is 68% GC throughout and has no anchor windows, so its estimate rests on the GC model alone and carries an offset of 17% between technologies at a pair SD of 0.040. The distal junction does not vary between people, so its intraclass correlation is near zero by construction; its within-person CV of 1.8% is the figure that matters.

The intraclass correlation measures absolute agreement, so an offset between technologies counts against it: the published depth ratio's −27% offset is a property of the library, not of the person, and removing it as a batch effect leaves an ICC of 0.87 against 0.98 for NGS-DOSE, whose offset is +2%. The two DNA batches were drawn from different cultures of each line, so these figures bound measurement error from above. This is the comparison that separates NGS-DOSE from the published depth ratio, and NGS-DOSE does better on every measure in the table: offset, pair SD, Pearson r, intraclass correlation, within-person CV. Within one chemistry (3.6) the difference cannot be seen.

3.5 What the fragment-GC model removes

Libraries differ in GC bias even within one chemistry: the rate at which 65%-GC fragments were sequenced, relative to each library's mean, runs from 1.18 to 1.29 across the middle 80% of genomes, and the rDNA is GC-rich. The published 18S depth ratio divided by NGS-DOSE's calibrated estimate of the same genome follows that bias with r = 0.85 (0.83 to 0.86) (n = 1,259); the same 18S region under NGS-DOSE's fragment-GC model, r = 0.07 (0.01 to 0.12). Within the cohort the effect is a few percent (SD of the log ratio 0.033), small next to the 22% by which people differ, which is why it does not show in the trios; between technologies (3.4) it is 27%.

3.6 Transmission in trios

A child's dosage is the mean of the parents' plus segregation; measurement error is not inherited. The midparent slope therefore measures the share of an estimate's variance that is real, its reliability, for each estimator separately. Two traits of the same genomes that are not transmitted run beside them as negative controls: held-out autosomal sequence, which has error but no true variance, and the mitochondrial and EBV content of the culture, which vary but are not in the nuclear genome.

252 complete trios.

How to read the numbers. Correlations are Pearson's, on values centred within population. The child–midparent correlation cannot reach 1 even for a perfectly measured heritable trait: half of a child's variance is segregation, which the midparent does not predict, so r is bounded by about √((1 + ρ)/2) — 0.74 at the 45S's spousal correlation of 0.10. The midparent slope b has no such ceiling (it is 1 when every unit of parental variance reappears in the children), which is why the slope, corrected for the spousal correlation to R = b − ρ(1 − b), is the number that answers "what share of the measured variance is real". Inference rests on the family-bootstrap interval of R; the permutation p-value (children shuffled among families) says whether a slope of that size arises by chance.

Every metric the cohort measures was put to the same test, in four groups: the rDNA estimators, whose transmission is the claim; the satellite arrays, whose mass is a property of the genome and must be inherited (positive controls); sequence of known copy number, which has nothing to inherit except the distal junction's whole-copy steps (3.2); and the culture's and the library's properties, which are not in the nuclear genome (negative controls). A method that measured library artefacts would light up the last group; one that measured nothing would light up none. HSat1B lives mostly on Yq and passes from father to son only, so its midparent statistics are diluted by design; the split by the sex of parent and child (below) tests it as it is inherited. The last column repeats the reliability with the cohort layer and the trio test run on the fetch counts alone (3.3).

Reliability is capped at 1; a slope above 1 is noise around 1, and the interval says how much. A spousal correlation far from zero means members of a family share something other than DNA (a batch), and every reliability in the table is inflated by about as much. The negative-control rows should read near zero.

The 45S reliability is 1.00 (0.93 to 1.21); the interval allows a measurement error of at most 5.9% of a person's value. The variation measured is therefore inherited. Because people differ in 45S copy number by a CV of 22% and every estimator errs by a few percent, every estimator has a reliability near 1 within one cohort and one pipeline, and the trios cannot rank them: the paired differences below are the test, and they are small. Ranking rests on the comparison across technologies (3.4).

By the sex of parent and child

The midparent test assumes that each parent passes on half of what they carry, as they do for sequence on the autosomes. Sequence on the sex chromosomes is inherited differently: a father passes his Y whole to his sons and none of it to his daughters, and his X whole to his daughters and none of it to his sons, while a mother passes one of her two X chromosomes to every child. Split by the sex of parent and child, the correlation of child with parent is therefore about one half in all four pairings for a well-measured autosomal quantity; close to 1 from father to son and 0 from father to daughter for a Y-linked one; 0 from father to son and high from father to daughter for an X-linked one. Correlations, not slopes, are compared here: a slope also carries the ratio of the child's spread to the parent's, which differs between men and women for a sex-linked quantity. Values are centred within population and sex, so that the difference between men and women is not read as transmission. 125 of the trios have a son and 127 a daughter, so each pairing rests on about half the trios and a correlation is uncertain by about ±0.15 (95%).

HSat1B array: father–son r = 0.93, father–daughter r = 0.12 (the difference is 11.8 standard errors on Fisher's scale). By that contrast this metric carries sequence on the Y chromosome: fathers pass more of it to their sons than to their daughters, and the midparent reliability above understates how faithfully it is inherited. Between two and three standard errors lie three of the 23 metrics, where chance alone would put about one (the held-out autosomal sequence, which has nothing to inherit, is a guide): bSat array, r 0.58 against 0.35 (z = 2.3); aSatHOR array, r 0.00 against 0.29 (z = −2.3); insert size, r −0.34 against −0.04 (z = −2.5). No other metric's father–son and father–daughter correlations differ by more than three standard errors.

Class by class

Every metric's transmission in the same terms: how much people differ (the trio parents' coefficient of variation, CV); the share of that difference the children inherit (R, with its 95% interval, as estimated rather than capped at 1 as in the tables above); the part of a person's value that is not inherited, as a percentage of the value (CV × √(1 − R): measurement error, or change in the cell line; the interval allows at most the figure in brackets); the children's spread and level against their parents'; and whether the four pairings of the parent's and the child's sex differ, which for a quantity carried on the autosomes they should not.

Parents and children were sequenced apart. All 252 children are among the 698 related genomes that the 1000 Genomes 30× release added to its original 2,504 (the release batch in NGS-PCA's table), and 489 of their 504 parents are among the 2,504; 13 families have a parent in the child's batch. A batch shared within a family, which could imitate inheritance, is therefore all but absent. But a difference between the batches is a difference between the generations. Where the later batch reads a quantity on a slightly larger or smaller scale, the children's spread changes, and the midparent slope and R change with it by the same factor, while R computed with the children's values first put on their parents' scale does not. New variation arising in the children would also widen their spread, and lowers the rescaled R instead; the two values bracket the reliability. They part where the children's spread departs furthest from their parents': sequencing depth, 0.54× (0.42 to 0.70); duplicate-flagged fraction, 1.59× (1.25 to 2.03); insert size, 0.75× (0.67 to 0.84); library GC bias, 1.25× (1.08 to 1.43); HSat2 array, 1.14× (1.04 to 1.23); ACRO array, 0.92× (0.84 to 1.00). The HSat2 array's wider spread cannot be new variation arising in the children, because its slope rises with it (R 1.02 to 1.28). Nor can the ACRO array's narrower one. New variation widens the children's spread and leaves the slope alone; a batch that reads the children on a slightly different scale moves both together. The Mendelian reliability shown in earlier versions of this page's table, 1.5 − Var(child − midparent) / Var(parent), equals R + 1 + ρ/2 − s², with s the ratio of spreads, so on this design it measured the batch: sequencing depth, which no child inherits (R = −0.05), reads 0.65 by it. It is no longer shown; data/transmission.tsv keeps it.

CV: how much people differ, the parents' standard deviation over their mean. R: from the midparent slope, and rescaled: with the children's values first put on their parents' spread (both with their 95% intervals in the figure). Not inherited: CV × √(1 − R) at the lower of the two, as a percentage of a person's value, and in brackets the most the intervals allow. Children's spread: their standard deviation over their parents'; children's level: their mean over their parents'; both on values centred within population, with 95% family-bootstrap intervals. Sex pairings: how often the four child–parent correlations (father–son, father–daughter, mother–son, mother–daughter) differ as much as these when the children's sexes are shuffled among the families and each family's parents swap roles (1,000 shuffles). The textbook test, which assumes normal values, is far too small for skewed ones (the distal junction's four pairings: 0.616 by it, 0.949 by the shuffles).

45S rDNA. The trio parents differ by a CV of 22%. The children inherit all of it that the trios can resolve: R = 1.07 (0.93 to 1.21) from the slope and 1.04 (0.95 to 1.12) with the children on their parents' scale, and at most 5.9% of a person's value is not inherited (the pilot's replicates across technologies put the measurement's own error at 2.3%, section 3.4). The child–midparent correlation, 0.77 (0.71 to 0.82), reaches the ceiling of 0.74 that segregation sets for a perfectly measured trait at the spousal correlation of 0.10 (−0.02 to 0.24). The father and the mother pass it on alike (child–father r = 0.58, child–mother r = 0.56), as they should for arrays on the short arms of five autosomes; split by the sex of parent and child, the four correlations are 0.55 (father–son), 0.63 (father–daughter), 0.45 (mother–son) and 0.65 (mother–daughter), no more different than chance makes them (p = 0.227). The children spread 1.03× as much as their parents (0.93 to 1.12) and read 5.1% more than their parents (+3.3% to +6.9%): a difference of generation or of batch, which this design cannot separate, and one the slopes and correlations, unchanged when every child is shifted by the same amount, do not see. An array is rearranged in more than one meiosis in ten (Stults et al. 2008). Rearrangement as likely to lengthen an array as to shorten it scatters the children about the midparent without flattening the slope, and widens their spread: if the batch changed nothing, by at most 25% of the parents' variance, the top of the interval. The batch alone moves the variance of the HSat2 array by 30%, so the trios bound that variation; they do not measure it.

5S rDNA. The parents differ as much as in the 45S (CV 24%), but the children inherit less of it, or less certainly: R = 0.90 (0.66 to 1.13), 0.83 (0.64 to 0.98) on the parents' scale, at a spousal correlation of 0.08. The interval runs from an array transmitted as faithfully as the 45S to one with 34% of its differences not inherited. New variation arising in the children at random would scatter them about the midparent line without flattening it (they spread 1.07× as much as their parents, 0.94 to 1.20). A slope below 1 means that part of the parents' measured differences is not passed on: error, change in the cell line, or arrays that drift toward the average as they are transmitted; 10% of a person's value at the estimate, at most 14%. The pilot's replicates across technologies put the measurement's own error near 2.8% (section 3.4), so at the estimate the part not inherited would lie in the cell lines or in transmission rather than in the measurement. The array is on chromosome 1 (1q42); split by the sex of parent and child, the four correlations are 0.38 (father–son), 0.52 (father–daughter), 0.52 (mother–son) and 0.39 (mother–daughter), no more different than chance makes them (p = 0.496).

Satellite arrays. Every class is inherited (permutation p ≤ 0.001). In every class whose children spread as their parents do, the part of a person's value that is not inherited lies between 2% and 9%, and how much of R that costs depends on how much people differ. The classes that vary least between people (SATR, CER and aSatHOR, CV 5.4% to 6.4%) read the lowest R (0.81, 0.87 and 0.33): the same few percent is a larger share of a smaller spread. Those that vary most (bSat, SST1, HSat3 and HSat1A, CV 12% to 18%) read 0.75 to 0.97. Two classes are read on a different scale in the children (above): HSat2 spreads 1.14× as much in the children as in their parents (1.04 to 1.23), and its R reads 1.15 from the slope but 1.01 on the parents' scale; ACRO spreads 0.92× as much in the children as in their parents (0.84 to 1.00), and its R reads 0.89 from the slope but 0.97 on the parents' scale. HSat1B lies mostly on the Y chromosome: it passes from father to son at r = 0.93 and to daughters at 0.12, which the midparent statistics do not measure (by sex, above).

Telomeric repeat. Weakly inherited: R = 0.36 (0.19 to 0.53), at the largest spread between people (CV 39%), so 31% of a person's value is not inherited. Telomeres shorten with age and change in culture; the children, younger than their parents and sequenced in the later batch, read 10.3% more than their parents (+5.5% to +15.3%).

Known copy number. Held-out autosomal sequence has nothing to inherit, and the children inherit nothing of it: R = −0.06 (−0.26 to 0.16), with people differing by 0.4%, the measurement's floor. The distal junction is 10 copies in most genomes; the whole-copy steps some carry (3.2) run in families and are inherited: R = 0.77 (0.47 to 1.06), people differing by 3.7%.

Culture and library. No property of the culture or the library is inherited: R runs from −0.58 to 0.30, and every interval but that of insert size (−0.77 to −0.38) includes zero; an interval wholly below zero is not inheritance, and one such interval among 23 metrics is what chance gives at 95%. These are also the metrics whose spread differs most between the generations (the children's sequencing depth varies 0.54× as much as their parents'): properties of the batch, not of the family.

3.7 Independent measurements: ddPCR, a published pipeline, coverage QC

An orthogonal assay: ddPCR

Potapova et al. (Cell Genomics 2025) measured 45S copy number by droplet digital PCR in lymphoblastoid lines, 12 of them 1000 Genomes or Genome in a Bottle lines with a NovaSeq genome (7 counted in this run; the rest fetched from the same CRAMs and calibrated with this cohort's saved efficiencies, or counted from a second NovaSeq pipeline, by the results repository's assembly_rdna study). The assay's own precision: median CV 5.0% between replicates. NGS-DOSE reads 0.957× the assay (mean absolute difference 4.9%), r = 0.95 (0.81 to 0.99), Spearman 0.97; the authors' own k-mer estimate, CONKORD, 0.994× (r = 0.87); the 18S depth ratio 1.093× (r = 0.93). The level is the first external check of the anchor windows: NGS-DOSE sits 4.6% below the assay, within what a dozen lines can resolve.

On the 954 genomes shared so far with Hall, Turner & Queitsch (2021), their 18S value against the same 18S depth ratio computed from NGS-DOSE's counts (no GC model), halved to their per-haploid scale: r = 0.985, their values 1.085× ours. Re-applying their exclusion of duplicate-flagged reads to our counts brings the ratio to 1.036 (SD 0.037): the offset is the duplicate flag, which marks fewer reads inside the collapsed rDNA than outside it (section 4). Against the calibrated estimate (rDNA45S.cn/2): r = 0.969, ratio 1.231.

NGS-PCA's coverage QC on the same files

NGS-PCA computes, from mosdepth coverage of the same CRAMs in 1-kb bins with duplicate-flagged reads excluded, mitochondrial copies per cell as twice the chrM mean coverage over the median autosomal coverage, and the X and Y coverage ratios. On the 1,259 shared genomes, mitochondrial copies per cell agree at r = 0.996 (0.995 to 0.996), theirs 0.923× ours (10–90% 0.900–0.940; SD of the log ratio 0.019); chrX at r = 0.9997, ratio 1.003; autosomal depth at r = 0.973, theirs 0.88× ours. Sex inferred by the two agrees in 1,258 of 1,259. The 19 women and 9 men whose cultures have lost part of an X or a Y read the same by both routes (for example HG00154: 1.32 here, 1.33 there). The chrY ratio in men is compressed and noisier by the coverage route (median 0.80 in men with an intact Y, r = 0.35 against our 40 X-degenerate regions), since a whole-chromosome mean includes sequence that maps poorly. The mitochondrial offset lies in the direction of the duplicate flag, which mosdepth honours and NGS-DOSE does not: a 16.6-kb genome at several thousand-fold depth saturates the positions a duplicate marker can distinguish, and the ratio falls with depth (r = -0.32).

3.8 Satellite arrays against long-read assemblies

The satellite arrays are measured by the same k-mer machinery as the rDNA, and unlike the rDNA they have a truth: 96 of the genomes counted so far belong to people with an HPRC release-2 assembly, built from long reads for both haplotypes, whose CenSat annotation gives the length of every satellite array. Summed over the two haplotypes, that is the person's array mass for each family, in megabases. NGS-DOSE estimates the same mass from the short reads, from the reads that carry the family's k-mers. The rDNA itself cannot be compared this way: the assemblies do not close its arrays (section 1).

If both measurements are right, a person's two values are equal. Where the k-mer panel sees only part of a family, NGS-DOSE reads the family low by about the same share in everyone, and the people lie on a line below equality. The panel's recall is the share of a family's reads it can assign in CHM13, the genome it was built from: bSat, SST1, CER and SATR have a recall well below 1 and are relative measures, comparable between people but not in absolute megabases. What tests the method is how closely each person sits on their family's line.

genomes
People compared in the family: counted here, with an HPRC release-2 assembly, and not left out.
left out (gaps)
An assembly does not always finish an array. Where it stops, the annotation marks a gap of unknown length labelled with the family (for example GAP,HSat2), and the assembly's mass for that family is then only a lower bound. A person is left out of a family's comparison when such gaps amount to more than 2% of the family's annotated mass in their assembly. An array the assembler collapsed or lost without leaving a gap cannot be seen this way.
median estimate / assembly
The typical ratio of NGS-DOSE's mass to the assembly's: near 1 for a family the panel sees fully, lower for a relative one.
SD of log ratio, robust SD
How far individual people scatter around that ratio, roughly the per-person disagreement as a fraction (0.05 is about 5%). The robust version, 1.4826 × the median absolute deviation, is not moved by a few outliers.
between-person CV, assembly
How much people differ in the family, by the assembly's measure: the variation the comparison has to reproduce.
Pearson r, Spearman
How well the order and spacing of people is reproduced (Spearman: the order only). r can be high only where people differ by much more than the two measurements disagree. r ≥ 0.95 is the mark the summary uses to say that a family tracks the assemblies: a round threshold set when six people could be compared, not a statistical test. By it, HSat1B track the assemblies.

A modest r does not mean poor agreement where people barely differ: aSatHOR arrays differ between people by 4.3% and the two measurements agree per genome to 4.0% (robust SD), so with so little to separate people r stays at 0.65. For SST1 and SATR the two measurements disagree per genome by more than people differ, so this comparison cannot test those panels. Of the 25 comparisons more than three robust SDs from their family's median (in HSat1A, HSat1B, HSat2, HSat3, aSatHOR, ACRO and CER), 21 are genomes whose assembly holds less than the reads show, the direction expected where part of an array is missing from an assembly without a marked gap.

3.9 Technical structure: coverage PCs

The residual depth of the 800 control regions after the GC model carries whatever library and sample structure is left; its principal components are technical covariates computed on sequence disjoint from every class. Marchenko-Pastur edge: 17 components clear the noise bulk (n = 800 x p = 1,259; edge 1.913 fitted on the leading 120 of 800 singular values; noise SD ~0.03; edge 1.11x as broad as equal-variance noise would make it).

Regressing out the 17 components above the edge removes this share of each estimate's variance (log scale), against what 17 random regressors would remove by chance:

columnvariance removedexpected by chanceadjusted R²
rDNA45S.cn1.998%1.351%0.655%
rDNA45S.cn_single1.842%1.351%0.498%
rDNA45S.18S.flat3.252%1.351%1.927%
rDNA5S.cn1.768%1.351%0.423%
DJ.cn17.089%1.351%15.953%
truth.auto30.635%1.351%29.685%
chrM.copies28.190%1.351%27.206%
chrEBV.copies18.968%1.351%17.858%

The components find technical variance where it exists: 31% of the held-out autosomal estimate's variance, which is nothing but error, against 2% of the 45S estimate's (1.4% expected by chance). With a measurement error of a few percent and a between-person CV of 22%, the technical share of the 45S variance is small; the GC model and the calibration do the work, and the PCs are insurance.

The sweep, 0 to 34 control PCs regressed out, cross-validated: the known truths say when adjustment stops removing noise; transmission (252 trios) says when it starts removing signal. One-standard-error picks: truth.auto: 3, truth.chrX: 7, truth.chrY: 0, DJ.cn: 5, rDNA45S.cn: 0, rDNA45S.cn_single: 0, rDNA45S.18S.flat: 0, rDNA5S.cn: 0.

NGS-PCA coverage PCs: Marchenko-Pastur edge: 40 components clear the noise bulk (n = 3,200 x p = 142,070; edge 54.72 fitted on the leading 200 of 200 singular values; noise SD ~0.126; edge 1.56x as broad as equal-variance noise would make it); 1,257 of the genomes have them.

The cell line

Every genome was sequenced from a lymphoblastoid cell line, whose state leaves marks on coverage. Mitochondrial genomes per cell: median 740 (10–90%: 599–940); EBV episomes per cell: median 42.0 (17.4–129.3). Both vary far more between people than the rDNA does and neither is inherited through the nuclear genome, which is why they serve as negative controls in 3.6.

Satellite arrays and the telomeric repeat

Satellite arrays are dispersed over the alignment, so only a whole-file scan measures them. Diploid mass per family; what each panel can see was measured on the genome it was built from (four families are relative measures, under-read by their k-mer recall).

5. Limitations

  • Absolute scale on a dozen lines. The one assay, ddPCR on 12 lines, reads NGS-DOSE 0.96× its value, 4.6% low; beyond those lines the level rests on unit windows on which three Illumina chemistries agree. The known truths test the model and the k-mer path, not the absolute scale of the rDNA.
  • Cell-line DNA. Every sample is a lymphoblastoid line; its replication state, EBV load and mitochondrial content are measured but not removed. Blood-derived genomes will not carry the first of these.
  • Generation and batch go together in the trios. Every child was sequenced in a later batch than its parents (3.6), so no batch is shared within a family to imitate inheritance, but a difference in the children's level or spread cannot be told from the batch's; R and R with the children on their parents' scale bracket the reliability. Because the rDNA varies far more between people than any estimator errs, trios show that the measured variation is real, not which estimator measures it best.
  • One chemistry, one pipeline. The cohort is NovaSeq 2×150 aligned by one pipeline; the cross-technology evidence is twelve genomes. DRAGEN alignments and other chemistries are untested.
  • The satellite panels were built from one genome (CHM13). Four of the ten families are relative measures; HSat2 agrees poorly with the 47 assemblies that close its arrays (r = 0.09, SD of the log ratio 0.29), though it is inherited as faithfully as the other classes (R = 1.01, 0.92 to 1.10, with the children on their parents' scale; 3.6): what it measures is heritable, but the assemblies do not yet confirm that it is the mass of HSat2. The telomere class is a relative measure of (TTAGGG)n content, not a telomere length.
  • Partial cohort. 1,259 of 3,202: population comparisons and the number of complete trios depend on which genomes have landed.

6. Data and reproducibility

The counts files under counts_scan/ and counts_fetch/ are the primary data: about 240 kB per whole-file scan and 70 kB per fetch, no reads, no genotypes. Everything above is computed from them:

pip install ngsdose        # or: apptainer pull ngs-dose.sif docker://ghcr.io/jlanej/ngs-dose:latest
ngsdose report --scan counts_scan/ --fetch counts_fetch/ -p pedigree.txt --hall hall2021_MOESM1.txt --pilot pilot/ --qc ngspca_sample_qc.tsv -o docs/

Tables behind every figure: data/cohort.tsv (one row per genome, every column), data/modes.tsv, data/transmission.tsv, data/transmission_by_sex.tsv and data/trios.tsv (every trio's values), data/fetch_check.tsv, data/pcsweep.tsv, data/satellites_hprc.tsv, data/rdna_hprc.tsv, data/flags.tsv; the numbers in the prose, report.json; the ddPCR lines, data/ddpcr.tsv; the trio assessment as a document, trio_report.pdf. The counts were made by ngs-dose count (0.1.0+fae1124 (1,259)) from the 1000 Genomes 30× CRAMs (Byrska-Bishop et al., Cell 2022; AWS Open Data) with the GRCh38-v1 resource bundle. Method, design document and audit: github.com/jlanej/NGS-DOSE.

Supplementary figures: every trio metric, child against midparent

One figure for each metric of the trio test (3.6), in its groups: x the mean of a child's two parents, y the child, on the natural scale; sons blue, daughters orange, each with its least-squares line, and the grey diagonal where child equals midparent. The statistics in each caption are those of 3.6, on values centred within population (and, for the split by sex, within sex too). 252 complete trios.
